en: Thus have I heard: the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the Eighteenth Discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Kapilavatthu for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, returning from his alms round, he went to the Great Forest for his midday rest.
Having entered deep into the Great Forest, he sat down at the foot of a beluva sapling for his midday rest.
Sakka, the wielder of the thunderbolt, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Great Forest.
Having entered deep into the Great Forest, he went to where the beluva sapling was, to where the Blessed One was; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, Daṇḍapāṇi Sakka stood leaning on his staff to one side. Standing there, he said this to the Blessed One:
“What does the ascetic profess, and what does he declare?
“Friend, as to how I speak and what I declare in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...”
“Friends, I am one who speaks thus and declares thus: ‘He does not stand in dispute with anyone in the world, including its gods and humans;

and as for that brahmin who dwells detached from sensual pleasures, free from doubt, with remorse cut away, and whose craving for becoming and non-becoming has vanished—perceptions do not adhere to him.’”
When this was said, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan shook his head, wagged his tongue, raised three lines on his forehead, and leaning on his staff, he departed.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the Nigrodha Park; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Here, monks, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Kapilavatthu for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu and returned from the almsround after the meal, I went to the Great Forest for my midday rest.
Having plunged deep into the Great Forest, I sat down at the foot of a beluva sapling for my midday rest.”
"Monks, while Sakka Daṇḍapāṇi was walking and wandering for exercise, he approached the Great Wood.
Having entered the Great Wood, he went to the Beluva tree where I was staying. Upon arrival, he exchanged greetings with me.
After exchanging polite and amiable words of greeting, he stood to one side leaning on his staff. Standing to one side, monks, Sakka Daṇḍapāṇi said this to me:"
"What does the ascetic profess?
What does he declare? When this was said, monks, I said this to Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan:
"In whatever way he speaks, friend, regarding this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins..."
‘In this world with its devas and humans, he does not stand in conflict with anyone;
and because that brahmin dwells detached from sensual pleasures, free from doubt, with remorse cut away, and with craving for becoming and non-becoming extinguished, perceptions do not adhere to him.
It is as one who speaks thus, friends, that I declare myself.’”
When this was said, monks, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan shook his head, lolled his tongue, raised a three-pronged wrinkle on his forehead, and leaning on his staff, he departed.
When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One:

“In what way, Bhante, does the Blessed One stand without quarreling with anyone in the world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans?”

"But how, venerable sir, is it that perceptions do not pursue the Blessed One— who dwells detached from sensual pleasures, who is free from doubt, whose remorse is cut away, and who is devoid of craving for existence and non-existence? "Monk,
wherever the conceptual proliferations of perception and designation pursue a person,
if therein there is nothing to be delighted in, nothing to be welcomed, and nothing to be clung to..."

This is the end of the underlying tendencies of lust; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of aversion; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of views; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of doubt;
this is the end of the underlying tendencies of conceit; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of lust for existence;
this is the end of the underlying tendencies of ignorance; this is the end of taking up sticks and weapons, of quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech.
"Here these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary and without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
'Bhikkhu, from whatever source proliferation, perception, and conceptualization beset a person...'"
“If there is nothing here to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to—
this indeed is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust...
it is here that these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.”
“Who might be able to analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed?
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“This venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates.”
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna regarding this matter?
Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna, and having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated there, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One, having given us a brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
'Bhikkhu, it is from whatever source that the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) beset a person.'"
“If there is nothing here to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to—
this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust...
it is here that these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.”
"Friend Kaccāna, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred to us:
'Friends, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
"Bhikkhu, it is from whatever source that the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) assail a person. "
“If there is nothing here to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to—
this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust...
it is here that these evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.”
"Who, indeed, could analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, friends Kaccāna, it occurred to us:
"This venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by wise companions in the holy life."
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One,
the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter?”
“Let the venerable Mahākaccāna explain it.
“Suppose, friend, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by the root and the trunk of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, looking for heartwood only among the branches and foliage.”

"Friends, you should consider that it is as if you were to think, 'This must be sought after,' when the Teacher is present before you, yet you bypass that Blessed One and think, 'This matter must be asked of us.

For that Blessed One, friends, knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata."
"That was indeed the right time for you to have asked the Blessed One about this matter yourselves.
You should have retained it exactly as the Blessed One would have explained it to you.

"Surely, friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata."
It was indeed the right time for us to have asked the Blessed One about this matter ourselves,
so that we might have remembered it exactly as the Blessed One would have explained it.
Nevertheless, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates.
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
Let the Venerable Mahākaccāna analyze it, without finding it troublesome.
“Therefore, friends, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:
“Friends, when the Blessed One had given us a brief summary of the teaching and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:”
“‘Bhikkhu, it is because of this that the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation beset a person.
If there is nothing here to be delighted in, welcomed, or adhered to, this is the very end of the underlying tendencies to lust...
[and so on] ...here these evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. It is regarding this, friend, that the Blessed One said to me:”
In brief, I understand the meaning in detail of this summary that has been recited but whose meaning has not yet been analyzed as follows:
"Friends, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling;
what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about..."
One proliferates; because one proliferates, from that as a source, the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation beset a person regarding forms cognizable by the eye, past, future, and present.
Likewise, friends, dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises... [and so on].
"Friends, dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises...
dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises...
dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises..."
"Friends, dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling.
What one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one proliferates through conceptual proliferation (*papañca*).
Because of what one proliferates, various perceptions and notions born of proliferation beset a person with regard to the past, future, and present."
Regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind:
"If, friends, the eye exists, visible forms exist, and eye-consciousness exists, it is possible that one will designate 'contact.
If contact is designated, it is possible that one will designate 'feeling.'"
When there is a designation of feeling, it is possible that he will designate a designation of perception.
When there is a designation of perception, it is possible that he will designate a designation of applied thought.
When there is a designation of applied thought, it is possible that he will designate a designation of the occurrence of the conceptual proliferation of perceptions and mental formations.
Thus, friends, when there is the ear and there is sound …pe… when there is the nose and there is odor …pe… when there is the tongue and there is taste …pe…
When there is the body, when there are tangible objects … [and so on] … when there is the mind,
when there are mental phenomena, when there is mind-consciousness, it is possible that one will designate “contact.
When there is the designation of contact, it is possible that one will designate “feeling.”
When there is the designation of feeling, it is possible that he will designate the designation of perception.
When there is the designation of perception, it is possible that he will designate the designation of thought.
When there is the designation of thought, it is possible that he will designate the designation of the occurrence of conceptual proliferation and perceptions.
"Thus, friends, when the eye is absent, forms are absent, and eye-consciousness is absent, it is impossible that one could designate 'contact.
When there is no designation of contact, it is impossible that one could designate 'feeling.
When there is no designation of feeling, it is impossible that one could designate 'perception.'"
"In the absence of the designation 'perception,' one will designate the 'designation of thought'—this is impossible.
In the absence of the designation 'thought,' one will designate the 'designation of the occurrence of the conceptualization of proliferation'—this is impossible.
Indeed, friends, in the absence of the ear, in the absence of sound... [and so on].
When there is no nose and no odor ... [and so on] ...
when there is no tongue and no taste ... [and so on] ...
when there is no body and no tangible object ... [and so on].
When the mind does not exist, when mental phenomena do not exist, and when mind-consciousness does not exist, that one will designate the designation of contact—this is impossible.
When the designation of contact does not exist, that one will designate the designation of feeling—this is impossible.
When the designation of feeling does not exist, that one will designate the designation of perception—this is impossible.
"It is impossible that, perception being unmanifested, one would manifest ideation;
it is impossible that, ideation being unmanifested, one would manifest the manifestation of the proliferation of perceptions and conceptualizations.
Friend, when the Blessed One had given us this brief summary and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling..."

“‘Bhikkhu, when the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation beset a person on account of a certain source, if therein there is nothing to be delighted in, nothing to be welcomed, and nothing to be adhered to,
this is the very end of the underlying tendencies to lust … [as before] … herein these evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
This, friends, is how I understand in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, which had not been explained in detail.”
"And yet, Venerable sirs, if you so desire, you should approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter.
You should bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it to you.
Then those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Venerable Mahākaccāna, rose from their seats.
They approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, when the Blessed One had given us a brief summary of the teaching and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling..."
“Bhikkhu, it is from this source that the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation beset a person.
If there is nothing here to be delighted in, welcomed, or adhered to,
this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust … [and so on] …”
"‘It is here that these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred to us:
‘Friends, the Blessed One has given us this brief summary of the teaching and, without explaining its meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling.’”
“Bhikkhu, it is because of this that the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation beset a person.
If there is nothing here to be delighted in, nothing to be welcomed, and nothing to be clung to—
this is the end of the underlying tendency to lust, this is the end of the underlying tendency to aversion, this is the end of the underlying tendency to views.”
This is the end of the underlying tendencies of doubt; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of conceit;

this is the end of the underlying tendencies of lust for existence; this is the end of the underlying tendencies of ignorance; this is the end of taking up sticks and weapons, of quarrels, disputes, contention, strife, calumny, and false speech.
It is here that these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.”
"Who indeed might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to us:
"This venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One,
the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail. What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and,
having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter?”
“Then, venerable sir, we approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, we questioned the Venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter.
It was by these ways, these phrases, and these syllables, venerable sir, that the meaning was analyzed for us by the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
“Wise, monks, is Mahākaccāna; of great wisdom, monks, is Mahākaccāna.”
“Bhikkhus, even if you were to question me about this matter, I would explain it in exactly the same way that Mahākaccāna has explained it.
This indeed is its meaning, and thus you should remember it.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, just as if a man overcome by hunger and weakness were to find a honey cake, whatever part of it he might taste, he would surely obtain a sweet flavor, a delightful one;

even so, venerable sir, when a bhikkhu of firm nature examines the meaning of this discourse on the Dhamma with wisdom from whatever perspective, he surely obtains gladness and surely obtains clarity of mind.
What is the name, venerable sir, of this discourse on the Dhamma?”
“Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Honeyball Discourse.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Gratified, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
